utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we can now resume. Who is the witness today? I see you have a new assistant with you. Would you introduce her to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, a new assistant that is ultimately going to take over for Emil van der Does de Willebois is Ijeoma Udo, and she will be working with us until the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We would like to wish her welcome and at the same time say good afternoon to our interpreters, to the Defence as well. Now, Mr. Kehoe, would you begin, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, and good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The name -- I hope it will be spelled properly, both for my colleagues and for myself, that is in the transcript. I want to make sure that there is no error in the transcript with the spelling of the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I-J-E-O-M-A and the last name is Udo, U-D-O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can begin now. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think all of us can congratulate you and France on the win yesterday. There were some bets on whether or not you were going to make it this morning but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kehoe, I didn't think that you were going to congratulate me in that nationalistic way, but I am touched by that of course. Every one knew that as far as the France-Croatia match was one that was of interest to everybody, I suppose that is what you are talking about. Thank you very much. We can now resume, but more seriously, since we are dealing with a serious case here, I can say to you, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Our next witness is a man by the name of Lee Whitworth. Mr. Whitworth was a captain in the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire during their tour of duty in Bosnia from May of 1993 until early November of 1993. Subsequent to the tour in Bosnia, Captain Whitworth resigned from the British military and has been in the education field as a teacher since that time. I will say, and he's rather a modest man, that he was awarded the Queen's Gallantry medal for his actions in Bosnia during his six-month stay. We will not, Mr. President and Your Honours, engage in a repetition of much of the testimony that Your Honours have heard concerning various events that took place during the tour of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire. What we would do with this witness and at the Prosecutor's request is to present the evidence in a more episodic fashion, that is, particular instances of this particular witness's experience that will tie in much of that has been raised by the Prosecution and also by the Defence during the months of trial we've been talking about, the six months of the Prince of Wales' Own tour. So in that sense, Mr. President, it will be a testimony that focuses on connections. This particular individual was a liaison officer with the Hotel Vitez. In that capacity, he met the Defendant on occasion, and most of the time he spent speaking with an individual by the name of Darko Gelic, G-E-L-I-C, Darko Gelic was the Defendant Blaskic's liaison officer and did the speaking for then Colonel Blaskic during this period of time. He will speak to you about the structure of the Hotel Vitez, he will speak to you about his observations concerning Blaskic as a commander, he will speak about the communication capabilities of the HVO during this time frame. In conjunction with this testimony, he will speak about the use of helicopters moving in and out of the Lasva Valley at one particular location controlled by the HVO. He will talk about the Defendant being a commander who was out on the ground at various points. He will then talk about some of the men in the HVO that Your Honours have heard of to date. He will talk about his rather shocking conversations with Anto Valenta in the Hotel Vitez, his meeting of Mario Cerkez and his dealing with Mario Cerkez, those will be the two prominent individuals that he will talk about at the outset. He will then talk about a conversation that took place in late May, 1993 concerning the Jokeri, the Jokeri being housed at the Bungalow just past Ahmici on the way to Busovaca, and he will talk about the conversations that he had with the Jokeri, their identification of an individual as their leader, that individual being Pasko Ljubesic, and the subsequent attempts by Mr. Whitworth to talk to Pasko Ljubesic, and how he can relate Ljubesic and the military police, and connect them with Darko Gelic and the Hotel Vitez vis-a-vis the Defendant. He will then testify as to the Jokers in an actual military operation. That military operation obviously was not the one observed -- Ahmici was not observed by this witness, but the attack on the village of Grbavica on the 7th and 8th of 1993 was observed by this witness, and he will talk about the participation of the Jokeri in that attack along with the participation of other HVO soldiers. He will then talk about the Vitezovi, his knowledge of Darko Kraljevic. Darko Kraljevic was under the command and control of the Defendant Blaskic and part of the HVO military structure, and to that end, he will not only describe what the role was of the Vitezovi but he will also describe the particular instance, an offensive operation, where the Vitezovi moved into Donji Vecerska and actually participated in an operation where they fought against the ABiH, defeated the ABiH, and subsequently the person who spoke to the media about that particular event in praiseworthy fashion was the Defendant's liaison officer, Darko Gelic. We will not go through a long participation, Your Honours, of Stari Vitez. We will talk about Stari Vitez to a minor degree in the sense of how this witness viewed Stari Vitez and how the HVO viewed Stari Vitez in light of many of the military activities that were going on in the valley. He will then be the individual who, with Darko Gelic, on Blaskic's word, recovered the trucks that were taken in the Convoy of Joy. That recitation will be quite brief. He will also talk about the investigation of Dobrila Kolaba as he was the individual that was on the scene, we've heard some testimony about the killing of Dobrila Kolaba, the BRITBAT interpreter by Brigadier Duncan, but this particular witness was one that was actually there on the scene. He will talk about the investigation and the conclusions by the HVO on Dobrila, and he will also talk about the conclusions of the killing of the UNHCR driver Boris and the actual firing point and the weapon that was employed. He will touch to some degree on the use of propaganda on behalf of the HVO and how the HVO, and specifically Cerkez, had control over much of what was played on the radio. Lastly, he will talk about the attack on Grbavica and the actual looting and burning that took place in Grbavica after it was secured. As you can see from the indictment, Mr. President and Your Honours, the Prosecutor doesn't charge that the attack on Grbavica was unlawful, but it was the destruction and plunder of property after the attack by Blaskic's soldiers that is the crime. Suffice it to say, Mr. President and Your Honours, the testimony of Mr. Whitworth will focus on any number of counts, virtually all of the counts, because in this episodic fashion, it will touch on connections between participation by individual units, that Your Honours have heard to date, as well as the connections back to the Defendant Blaskic. The only actual attack he will talk about in some detail is the attack on Grbavica on the 7th and 8th of 1993. In any event, virtually all of the counts in the indictment, certainly the persecution count in Count 1, the wilful killing and serious injury in Counts 5 through 10, the destruction and plunder of property, Counts 11 through 13, and destruction of religious monuments to some degree as he will be unable to testify directly of the burning of the mosque in Grbavica, but he will testify that all of the individual structures around it were burning at the time. That is basically the presentation to be made by Mr. Whitworth. As I noted at the outset, it is basically testimony that connects various people and events that we have spoken about to date, and that would be the Prosecutor's presentation at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: About how long do you expect this to take, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say, Mr. President, probably a couple hours, I would think, depending --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you say a few hours, what do you mean? A couple of hours? What does that mean, a couple of hours? That could go from two to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Closer to two than 24. No, I'm kidding. Probably two and a half hours in toto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's it, two and a half hours. What I would like to ask you, in light of all of the questions that are going to be asked, is for you to focus on what is most important in the testimony. Please do not forget that if it's a long examination, if you have the witness speak about all of the subjects, necessarily we're going to have a long cross-examination and it will be very complicated and very subtle discussions in order to know whether the cross-examination is going to be on the scope of the direct examination. Therefore, Mr. Kehoe, please try to focus on the essential points. A witness is not a witness to everything that he saw throughout his stay. If you want to make him that, you can, of course, but then it's going to take very, very long. Try to be as concise as possible. Thank you very much. The witness can now be brought in (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me? Would you tell us your name and your given names and what your rank was at the time of the events, and then please remain standing until you have read your oath, and after that, you might be seated. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Captain Lee Whitworth, a Captain and liaison officer with the 1st Battalion Prince Of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire during the battalion's tour in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Read the oath, please, the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. Please be seated. You have been called to this Tribunal as part of the trial of General Blaskic who is in this courtroom now and whom you knew at the time. Mr. Kehoe is going to ask you several questions. Please testify freely. He has given us the general framework of your testimony. Please answer as close to the questions as you can. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, counsel. Good afternoon, Captain. Captain, you noted at the outset of your testimony that you were formerly a member of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire and a liaison officer, I believe, during the six-month tour in Bosnia from May of 1993 through early November 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am pausing one moment just to allow the interpreters to catch up. You and I have spoken about that before. Also I would ask you, when you are testifying, to direct your attention to the Judges. Captain Whitworth, tell the Judges about your military career, time of service, what you did in the service, and the specifics concerning your role as a liaison officer in Bosnia during your six-month tour?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was -- prior to Bosnia, I was serving in Northern Ireland, working and liaising with the Royal Ulster Constabulary. On my initial deployment to Bosnia, I was employed as the regimental signals officer, that is responsible for the communications and running of headquarters of the battalion. It was only after a period of two or three weeks, after the Colonel had reassessed the situation in the Lasva Valley, that he directed that we would have several of the liaison officers and I was appointed as the liaison officer to the Vitez-Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as liaison officer to Vitez and the Lasva Valley area, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was effectively the eyes and ears of the Colonel, and my job really was to develop a rapport and relationship with the people on the ground in order to facilitate our mission in supporting the UNHCR on their delivery of humanitarian aid to the people in the Lasva-Central Bosnia area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of that, Captain, did you become familiar with the Hotel Vitez and the various personalities in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed, sir. The Hotel Vitez was pretty much a pivotal point as far as I was concerned, there were several key personnel in there who held great prominence in the Lasva Valley area, primarily Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour there, did you meet the Defendant Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed, sir, on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were mostly your dealings with his liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A good number of those dealings were not with Colonel Blaskic directly but his personal liaison officer who was Darko Gelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can, we might as well start moving in through the photographs that we have identified, if we can, with the assistance of the usher, just pull out the first four photographs in the batch that we have? And Mr. Dubuisson, the photograph series is ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 432.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move these in series. Now, Captain, where is that photograph taken and are you in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That photograph is the front steps of the Hotel Vitez in the centre of Vitez itself. It was the operational headquarters of the HVO military command and military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is, in fact, the military police insignia on the front of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is. I can't see it very well on my screen, but it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just stop at some point. Counsel doesn't have his copies of his photographs, so before I move ahead, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is you, is it not, in the lower left-hand corner with the beret on?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, it is, and one of my drivers sat on the steps also with several members of the military police and HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph. The next photograph I believe would be 432/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a photograph that's taken inside the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Why is it 432/2? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think there are about 40 photographs, so it's going to be 432/1 for the first, then/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then the whole series represents Exhibit 432; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And there will be slash 1, 2, 3. So this is 432/2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This photograph, 432/2, is that a photograph with you and other military policemen inside the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, sir, yeah, in the foyer/entrance area.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correction. No, it's 433/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. 433.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 433/3, the next one, sir. Now, is that likewise taken inside the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is indeed, with Darko Gelic, the liaison officer for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you use your pointer and point to Darko Gelic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: (indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is to your right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next photograph, 433/4. Again, is that you and Darko Gelic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's Darko and myself and that's on the road outside Vitez (indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain, during your period of time there, did you become very comfortable walking around the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with the communication capabilities that were located in the Hotel Vitez and elsewhere that were available to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They had a system of -- they had computers in there, fax facility, telephone, and what appeared to be some form of transmittable radio/telephone system in there which didn't require telephone lines to operate, but they also had workable telephone lines going in and out of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other communication capabilities in and around the Hotel Vitez or the Lasva Valley that indicated to you the ability of the Defendant to communicate with his troops in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were -- there was also -- had the ability to transmit radio, there was a local radio station, they also had the ability to receive satellite television, and as I think -- I hoped I explained earlier, they seemed to have some system of satellite telecommunications, i.e. telephone system as well as the computers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain, during your tour, you said that you met the Defendant. Did you come to have some understanding as to what type of commander the Defendant was, and by that I mean, did he spend all his time in the Hotel Vitez? Was he a commander who was out on the ground inspecting his troops or consulting with them? I mean, what's been your experience?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic seemed a very active commander, he seemed to be well-informed, had a very good understanding of the situation, not just in the Lasva Valley area but also up and down all the HVO pockets as far as Vares. Often, when delivering messages for my own Colonel, it would be impossible for me to see Colonel Blaskic, I would be given the excuse that he wasn't in the building, he was out with the troops or he would be out at some other location in and around the Lasva area, and that was one of the reasons I didn't meet him directly as many times as I was instructed by my Colonel, and I also had the opportunity to meet him in other areas up and down the Lasva Valley, so he was quite active in terms of not centrally located on all occasions in the Hotel Vitez, taking an active role as the commander in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion, Captain, to meet the Defendant at a headquarters other than the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On one particular occasion, prior to the fall of the Travnik area, I met Colonel Blaskic in what looked like an operational headquarters location which was out of the Hotel Vitez and located near the wood yard forward toward the Travnik, Novi Travnik area. He was supported by his usual entourage of military police protecting that particular tactical headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he upset in any way that you had found him in this forward headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was extremely upset as was his liaison officer, Darko Gelic, who I had managed to trick, as it were, into leading me to him in the first place. Darko was very worried because he appreciated that Colonel Blaskic didn't want people to bother him at this particular location because obviously it was a very busy time at this tactical headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted, Captain, that Blaskic was in contact with other areas in his area of command. Did he, in fact, use Darko Gelic to introduce you to other individuals within his area of command?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were numerous occasions when, for example, if I wanted to do any particular work in an area, then Darko Gelic would be assigned to me as Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer, and Darko would then assist me in gaining access to particular areas that would have otherwise been difficult had I not had a senior HVO liaison officer and representative of Colonel Blaskic with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, let's turn our attention to 433/5, and if we can put that on the ELMO? Now, that is Darko Gelic in the blue shirt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening here?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This was -- Darko had taken me over to introduce me to commander Grubesic, who was the brigade commander in the Busovaca area, and the chap on the right of Darko, i.e. on the left of the photograph, is Commander Grubesic in the white T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can stay there, usher, and I just want to ask you about some capabilities of travel inside and out of the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, sir, when the Defendant and the HVO had capabilities of moving in and out of the Lasva Valley by air?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's the -- there were very, very frequent helicopter movements, HVO helicopter movements, in and out of the Lasva Valley despite the U.N. restriction of air movement. HIP helicopters would come in once, maybe twice a week, land by a quarry facility not far away from the British battalion location, stay for five to ten minutes, and leave, and there were periods of time when Colonel Blaskic was unavailable for us to speak to, but we assumed that he was moving, very probably moving in and out of the area to discuss matters with other commanders in the Kiseljak area or maybe down south in Prozor area. That is purely supposition, but it became very difficult to ascertain his location at times, and that was an assumption on our part that was quite feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before I move to the next photograph, if, Mr. Dubuisson, I could move to this particular map? And I believe that will be Exhibit 434.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, 434.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit 434, of course, Mr. President and Your Honours, is a portion of Exhibit 172. The area is circled to the right of this. Did you identify that location as the spot that the helicopter came and went from?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: On several occasions, that area, yes, was identified as the place where the helicopter was actually landing and taking off from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to slow down a little bit, please, for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the pointer, Captain, could you point to where the British battalion base was, and you are pointing to that area on the left-hand side of the photo.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: (indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this area that is circled as a helipad, why do you believe that area was chosen?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Because of the nature of the ground around that area, it would have been very difficult for BiH troops in the area to engage the helicopter with direct fire weapons or indirect fire weapons once it was on the ground because there were hill features around it, so the helicopters always engaged -- were engaged by some small arms on the way, but once it actually touched down, they were out of sight whilst static on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The helicopter coming in and going out was still fired on by Armija soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Indeed it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can, Mr. Usher, if we can move back to our series of photographs 433/6, I believe. Now, Captain, 436/6 is a photograph that was taken by you in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this some of the evacuation of medical wounded from Kiseljak to some other location?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this was a helicopter lift from Kiseljak. I organised the vehicle evacuation from Novi Bila hospital to Kiseljak, and the HVO liaison officers and officers in Kiseljak then arranged for an HV helicopter to pick up those casualties and take them further south to Croatia for medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, was this the type of helicopter or variations of this helicopter that -- the ones that flew into the quarry area that you just described on the prior exhibit?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next photograph which should be 433/7. Did you take that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's one of the helicopters spiralling down into the motion quarry area that we indicated on the map earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me change subjects, if you will, and if I can ask the usher just to remain there for one moment. During the period of time you had the opportunity to observe the HVO and the operation of the HVO, was there a chain of command?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was a very comprehensive chain of command, sir, yes. Colonel Blaskic was the senior military figure in the Lasva Valley area, and he had numerous subordinate brigade commanders and sub-unit commanders in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he appear to be taking steps to train his troops as well as other steps to defend the Lasva Valley area during the period of time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, on a few occasions we came across what appeared to be young soldiers being trained up to take their place as members of the local militia and brigades defending the Lasva pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to 433/8. Again, is that another photograph that was taken by you, captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Several young men I assessed at about the age of 15, 16, some a little bit older, in military uniform, formed up as a squad marching up the road, and that's just outside the wood yard area near one of the tactical headquarter locations that Colonel Blaskic had used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, based on your military experience, is that type of training you, as an officer, would expect to see with an army in theatre?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also noted that Blaskic was an effective commander in the defence of the Vitez area, and that included a large trenching system, did it not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, there was a very comprehensive series of trenches laid out around the -- all areas of the Lasva pocket. There were also detailed secondary defensive trenches which made it very difficult for the Armija to make any progress, so it was obviously a very carefully planned defensive system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just show you an example of some of this trenching system, a photograph that you took, 433/9. Is that one such photograph of an HVO trench that you took during your tour?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I can change subjects with you and move, Captain, to some of the personalities, and I'm just going to take a little bit of a break from those photographs, Mr. Usher, and to move to some photographs that were in evidence. The first photograph that I would like to talk to you about is a -- if I may, Mr. Dubuisson, this is part of Exhibit 80, eight zero.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is Exhibit 80/8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Whitworth, these photos of these HVO leaders are a series of photographs that were taken by you, were they not, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They are indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within these photos, is an individual by the name of Anto Valenta depicted?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's Mr. Valenta there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're pointing to the man with the moustache carrying the suitcase on the left half of that photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion early in your tour, Captain, to meet with Valenta and to discuss the political goals of the HVO and the Lasva Valley, and if so, tell the Judges in your own words what was that conversation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: During the early part of my tour, I was introduced to Anto Valenta by mayor Santic and Pero Skopljak, some political leaders. They took me to the Hotel Vitez and introduced me to Mr. Valenta as the new liaison officer for UNPROFOR in the Vitez area. Mr. Valenta went into great detail and described to me, using a series of maps and diagrams, what was happening in the area and what the future intentions as far as he was concerned were. That involved using a map and indicating to me an area of Central Bosnia that was covered in pie charts depicting the current distribution of different ethnic groups. The pie chart would show the percentage of Serbs, the percentage of Muslims, the percentage of Croats in each of the large towns, and Mr. Valenta then indicated the area that, as far as he was concerned, was going to be in the near future declared as Herceg-Bosna and indicated to me that this would be an entirely Croat area, not as it was then with three different ethnic groups of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats living in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that shock you, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It shocked me a great deal as it was at the beginning of my time in Bosnia and it was contradictory to what the U.N. had been working to and what the politicians in various organisations had said that they were working towards, it contradicted all those things that we expected to hear from a character who was allegedly the most senior political Croatian figure in the Lasva Valley at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, where was Valenta's office?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was in the Hotel Vitez on the ground floor just a little bit down from the place I met Colonel Blaskic on several occasions, the place I came to know as his office or working place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Captain, did you come to any conclusions in what regard Valenta was held by the other members of the HVO in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Valenta was seen as a key political figure, a figure who was revered, as far as I saw it, by the Croatian people in general, and also one of the policymakers in the Lasva Valley area as far as dictating military -- he obviously had an influence on military activity in the area. That was certainly the impression I got because of his proximity to Colonel Blaskic, the key military personnel in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us now touch on another personality, and if I may have, Mr. Dubuisson, Exhibit 254? Mr. Usher, it's this photograph (indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, do you know that individual?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's Mr. Mario Cerkez, a commander of the Vitez brigade, i.e., the local militia commander in the centre of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the Vitez brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he subordinate to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was one of Colonel Blaskic's brigade commanders, that's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Blaskic and Kordic relate to one another or did you see -- let me take -- in the Convoy of Joy situation, did you see Blaskic and Cerkez -- did I say Kordic? I apologise. Did you ever see Blaskic and Cerkez relate to one another?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: On one particular occasion during the Convoy of Joy, Colonel Blaskic was attempting to bring all the elements of the Convoy of Joy together and assist it on its way up towards the Tuzla area. There had obviously been considerable disruption to the convoy by the local civilians and HVO and pressure from Ambassador Thebault and Colonel Alastair, along with Colonel Blaskic, were literally going around trying to pressure people into releasing the vehicles so the convoy could re-form. On this particular occasion, at the Vitez checkpoint, Colonel Blaskic was trying to defuse the situation with a lot of Croatian civilians, and I could make out Commander Cerkez in the background trying to avoid being seen but nevertheless a witness, witness what was taking place. When Colonel Blaskic noted the presence of Commander Cerkez, he reprimanded him very strongly in front of the crowd of people and told him that what was happening to the Convoy of Joy was wrong and that he was to assist in releasing the vehicles and encouraged the local civilian population to do likewise. Commander Cerkez wasn't particularly happy or enthusiastic about this idea but nevertheless concurred with Colonel Blaskic's wishes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it clear to you that Cerkez was a subordinate to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I had always thought that, and that instance was, for me, said exactly that, whilst Commander Cerkez was at times disrespectful of Colonel Blaskic and didn't always like what he wanted to happen, nevertheless, as his superior commander, he obeyed when directed to by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And based on the word of Blaskic, did you recover the trucks that were taken from the Convoy of Joy with the assistance of Darko Gelic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Darko Gelic and another one of the staff from the Hotel Vitez, one of Colonel Blaskic's staff, assisted me for the following two or three days in visiting all the HVO and local militia that were holding the vehicles and Darko and another HVO representative from the Hotel Vitez assisted me in getting those vehicles released and reforming the Convoy of Joy so they could move north of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they obey, did the HVO local authorities obey the order of Blaskic as conveyed by Gelic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going to move to another subject, Captain, and the subject I'd like to talk to you about begins with a photograph 152? It's this photograph (indicated).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 152/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may put the larger one on there, it's a little easier to see. Now, Captain, I know you recognise that rather handsome chap depicted in that photograph as a colleague of yours, now Major Bower; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for the purposes of our testimony, we're going to be talking about the building that is situated behind Major Bower in this photograph, and I ask you, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. It was a building we referred to as the Swiss cottage, the French alpine hut, we used some other names, and it was on the road at Nadioci on the main road between Zenica and Vitez, a place called Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And several hundred metres from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, several hundred metres from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Early on in your tour, did you have the opportunity to go to this location and talk to the soldiers that were garrisoned in that building?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. During the early days of my tour as a liaison officer, I took it upon myself to drive around to familiarise myself with all the different parts and soldiers and commanders in the area. On one particular occasion, I noticed several youngish soldiers sat on the balcony area of the alpine hut, so I drove up in my Land Rover with my interpreter, got out, and tried to make conversation with them. Initially, this was very successful. I talked to several young soldiers, all of whom were dressed in black carrying large knives, maybe one or two hand guns apiece, and there were plenty of weapons. Actually inside the building and on the porch area. A gentleman of similar description but slightly older kept coming out of the back of the cottage and looked at me with disdain and obviously was not happy about me talking and making conversation with the younger chaps on the front. He made some reference to my interpreter, who was Muslim, and the situation got a little bit tense, but after calming that down, they divulged to me that they were part of an elite military police unit they described as the Jokeri, and they boasted quite happily about the fact that they had been involved in all the major HVO successes and offensive operations in and around the Busovaca-Vitez-Lasva Valley area. Throughout this, a gentleman kept coming out the back, again grunting and making comments to the effect that the chaps that sat on the front shouldn't be talking and divulging this information to me. I asked them -- I introduced myself as the liaison officer and said to them that, you know, it would be of use to me and maybe I might be of assistance to them if I was to meet their commander. They told me his name was a gentleman named Pasko and I should go to Vitez and look for him, and at this particular point the chap came out of the back and said that enough was enough and I had to leave and the younger gentlemen shouldn't talk to me any further. On that particular occasion, I then went into Vitez to continue exploring the sort of HVO hierarchy in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we talk about that, can you use this photograph and the pointer and just tell the Judges exactly where this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It took place actually on the balcony, up here (indicated). So I could see quite plainly into the actual Swiss cottage itself, and we sat on chairs out front with five or six members of the Jokeri, the elite military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, how long did this conversation go on for?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was there for approximately 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain, did they indicate to you anything about Ahmici or did you reach any conclusions about their participation in Ahmici after this discussion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At the time they said to me, they elaborated on the fact that they had been involved in all the major successful military operations, and I actually mentioned Ahmici, and they said -- they reiterated to me that it was all the successful military operations, so I took it from that that, yes, they were directly involved in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue on, Captain. You said after this conversation you went back into Vitez to try to continue to find out who the leader was of this organisation. Can you tell the Judges what you did?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I had already been directed to Hotel Vitez and Vitez area by these young members of the Jokeri. I had already made contact there, so I decided to use this as an excuse to introduce myself to the civilian police. I introduced myself to them, and they directed me to the Hotel Vitez and said I need to speak to the senior military police commander in the Hotel Vitez. They weren't actually part of the Jokeri, but the commander of such would be found or the gentleman responsible for them would be found in the Hotel Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me follow up something you just said. Who was not part of the Jokeri?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The normal civilian police, which is whom I had visited to explore who the commander was of the Jokeri, this Pasko chap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Jokeri was part of the military police?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, so I used this as a way of brokering myself into the local civilian police, but they directed me quickly over to Hotel Vitez and said that I would find the chief of military police in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is the same location that has "Military Police" on the front of it as we saw in one of the initial photographs that I believe was 433/1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go in there and meet a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I went in and asked if I could speak -- introduced myself to the senior military policeman because he was obviously a key figurehead in the area that I needed to be familiar with, and after -- after a brief wait, a gentleman, maybe late 40s, early 50s, bald head came to me and looked disdainfully and disinterested at me, wasn't really interested in meeting me, but introduced himself as one of the senior military police figures in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit 258, this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, do you recognise Exhibit 258?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was the gentleman who was introduced to me as one of the senior military police figures in the Hotel Vitez, I think his name is Vlado.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting, did you come to certain conclusions about the connection between the military police and the Jokeri?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did so and I reported that I had met the Jokeri and as far as I was concerned that they were a sub-unit based in the Lasva area, but their command was located in Hotel Vitez as part of the HVO hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you, in the presence of Darko Gelic, were finally introduced to this individual, Pasko, who was head of the military police?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir. One of my functions as liaison officer was to supervise the delivery of humanitarian aid, and during a particular part of the tour, there was a lot of tension. Consequently, the HVO insisted that they would only allow aid to be delivered to the Muslim areas as long as it was delivered simultaneously to the Croat area of Vitez, and this would only happen after the vehicles had been inspected by the senior military police commander. I arranged for the delivery to Vitez, the vehicles turned up, and Darko Gelic introduced me to a gentleman named Pasko Ljubesic who Darko introduced him as the senior military police commander from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it clear to you at this point that Darko was working together with Pasko on this?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir, yes. He was again a sub-unit commander, part of the HVO based in the Hotel Vitez, and was a very close liaison between him and Darko Gelic, Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it also clear to you, Captain, that this Pasko was the Pasko who was also the overall commander of the Jokeri?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir. Pasko was the name, first name I had been initially given by the Jokeri on my first meeting with them, and it fitted the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention, Mr. Dubuisson, to photographs 255 and 256.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, if I may, I'd like to show you a series of photographs, two photographs. If we can get over to the left a little bit? The chap is not -- there he is, okay. See it on the screen, Mr. Usher? Okay. That's good. That's good. That's great. This is Exhibit 255, and this again is another photograph that was taken by you, was it not, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the individual in the right-hand side of this photo?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was the chap introduced to me by Darko Gelic as Pasko Ljubesic, commander of the military police in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, if I may, Mr. Usher, the next photograph, 256? How about the individuals in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is Darko Gelic, Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me a second. Can you put the pointer on? That is the individual in the uniform to the left talking to the blue uniformed gentleman in the back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes. And that's Pasko Ljubesic (indicated) and these were the two local policemen who were just on the checkpoint who were just being informed of what was actually happening but weren't actually involved in the search themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This individual -- this photograph was taken by you as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was indeed, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you observed with me a videotape of an event where various individuals have been identified by you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, just go to the clip that is 270, we would ask for a still, but I think the Defence counsel had a still of Mr. Ljubesic. If I could just have Defence counsel's number, I don't really understand -- know the number we had on that. We can take another one or take the Defence's Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are you going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your position here, Mr. Kehoe? I didn't quite understand. What do you want to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll play the video and then stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the cassette 270; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question to you, Captain, is: Does that video, and I realise there is more on the video, does that appear to be the inside of the Swiss chalet?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I examined it closely, sir, earlier on, and it does appear to be what looked like the inside of the Swiss chalet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go back on the monitor, the still on the monitor? That individual, do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's Pasko Ljubesic, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the individual that you previously met or you had met after with Darko Gelic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That particular still is a still that was put into evidence by Defence counsel last week, and for the purposes of the record, we can just duplicate that effort as opposed to taking yet another still. There's no need to clutter up the record in that regard, counsel, I really don't know what the number is, but we can clarify it later. If we can continue on with that video? Better still, can you go back a little bit, just back a bit to the prior person on that video. Just a little bit? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That man, do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm quite -- I'm reasonably as certain as I can be bearing in mind the length of time that that was one of the gentleman I spoke to, sat on the front of the Swiss cottage that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we continue to play? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. How about the individual -- the bald individual with the hand on his head?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm as certain as I can be that that's the gentleman that I was introduced to as one of the senior military police officers in the Hotel Vitez that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Jokers informed you that they were involved in the HVO military successes in the Lasva Valley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They indeed, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification sake, approximately when was this conversation you had with these Jokers?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was very early on in my tour, I think it was about the end of May, beginning of June, 28th, 29th of May, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thereafter, Captain, did you see members of the Jokeri involved in any other HVO military successes in the Lasva Valley after that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Towards the end of our tour, during the HVO assault on Grbavica, I came -- I saw several gentlemen dressed in exactly the same manner, i.e. all in black, similarly well-equipped, who looked very familiar in terms of -- I was quite confident that they were members of the Jokeri that I had spoken to earlier on a few months earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This attack on Grbavica was when?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: 7th, 8th September, beginning of September area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted just previously that based on this, there was a connection between the Jokeri, as part of the military police, and the military police in the Hotel Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Blaskic? Did you see these military policemen in Blaskic's presence on occasion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, whenever he appeared on the ground, if there was some senior U.N. dignitary in the Lasva Valley, Colonel Blaskic would appear as a senior HVO commander and he would always be escorted and guarded by members of the military police unit based in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn ourselves to some photographs, and if we can go to this one? Is there a number on the back of that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go a little bit out of sequence here, 433/12. Do you recognise that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's a photograph I took when Cedric Thornberry was visiting Novi Bila hospital. That's Colonel Blaskic in attendance, Colonel Alastair, and Cedric Thornbury visiting and assessing circumstances of the Novi Bila hospital. And those are the military policemen who were in abundance around the hospital during Colonel Blaskic's visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it quite normal to see these military policemen in and about when Blaskic was present?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about an instance involving the local command and also the military police in the area of Rijeka (phoen) in early June of 1993. Do you remember an instance of maybe 30 Bosnian Muslims being held in the Rijeka area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I came across twenty to thirty, what were actually DPs, Displaced Persons, that weren't actually native of the Lasva Valley, and they were being accommodated in a group of houses in the area of Rijeka. They were all Muslims and the HVO/BiH frontline was a couple of hundred metres up the same road. When I found them there, I decided and spoke to them that they weren't in a very good situation, and I asked them what they would like to do. They said that they would like to go to Zenica where they had relatives, but they were being prevented from leaving the area by the local HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go ahead with the story, if I can show you this particular map, and I believe our next exhibit is ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you permit me to, do you want a freeze from the video clip, or do you want a new number for the cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The cassette is 270, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then it would be 270C, and the next number is 435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So the cassette keeps its original number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it keeps its original number, there's A and B for the French and English transcripts, and then C for the extract that we saw now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Whitworth, I show you Exhibit 435, an area circled in green at the top of the photograph. Is that the general area where these people were kept?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far from the frontline was that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Two, three hundred metres. I think it's also important to point out, they weren't actually being held within buildings, they weren't actually prisoners, they were just free to -- left to roam around that particular area but they weren't allowed to move from the area of those houses. They were provided with everything they needed but weren't actually kept as prisoners. There were actually 5 or 6 families of people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you this next photograph which should be 433/10. Does that photograph depict the area that is right near the frontline where these individuals were kept, where they were being held although being allowed to walk around?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were, sir, yes. They're basic hollow houses, and in the distance behind the Land Rover, as the track goes up, you can see that there are mines along the road because just over that horizon was the declared frontline area between the HVO and the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they being held for, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That wasn't immediately apparent to me, but it seemed like they were there as a deterrent to the BiH to not assault that particular avenue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you determine that they were being used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I went to see Mario Cerkez, the local brigade commander, because the soldiers in that area were under his direct command. He said -- he wasn't really interested, it was of no concern to him. He assured me that they were free to go where they wanted, but that was obviously not the case, and he was pretty disinterested about the whole thing. I then spoke to -- went to the Hotel Vitez and tried to address the matter to Darko Gelic, and he said again that they were free to move as and when they wanted to, so I promptly went back up to BRITBAT, got two Warriors and my Land Rover, and then went back to Rijeka and attempted to give them an opportunity to walk out in whatever direction that they chose with me as a guide. As we tried to leave, several members of the local militia HVO appeared, as did a vehicle with several military police and said that they were not -- the Muslims are not allowed to go anywhere, that they were to stay in the Rijeka area. So at that point, after getting extremely angry and annoyed, I then went to address the matter to the mayor, Mr. Santic, and he appreciated that it was a difficult circumstance and he would look into it, and then I spoke to Hotel Vitez again and said that what they had told me was not true, that I had been stopped by military police escorting them or assisting them in going wherever they wanted to in the Lasva area. I left the matter that particular day and went back a couple of days later to see if the circumstances had changed, and on my return, all the Muslims had left and it wasn't till two or three months later, after questioning people in Zenica that actually managed to make contact with several of them, and it would appear that the HVO had actually allowed them to leave the area and walk up over the mountain road into the Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain, this is the participation of two arms of the military, the local HVO and the military police from the Hotel Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the military commander above both of those units?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The military police were based in the Hotel Vitez, and Mario Cerkez, the brigade commander for the Vitez area answered directly to Colonel Blaskic's file, as far as I was concerned, so ultimately he was responsible for that troops' action on that particular day stopping the Muslims leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you reach conclusions that who, in the military structure, ordered that these people could leave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think -- I concluded that basically after I had pointed out the fact that these people could be construed as being used as a human shield, it became a bit of an embarrassment to the HVO, and the necessary orders were -- must have been issued by the Hotel Vitez to allow them to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move to the next point, Captain, on the military police and their sub-units, the Jokeri, based on what you've told us about your conversations with the Jokeri, about your conversations in the Hotel Vitez with Vlado Santic, your meeting with Pasko Ljubesic, with Darko Gelic, the activity of the Jokeri in the offensive operation in Grbavica, and lastly, the release of individuals who were formally being stopped from leaving by the local HVO and the military police, based on all those facts, did you reach any conclusions on what command Blaskic had over these military police in theatre?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Commander Blaskic had the ultimate command over the military police as far as I was concerned and of the brigade commanders in the Lasva area. He had obviously lots of strategic considerations outside the Lasva Valley -- the valley area, but he ultimately demonstrated on numerous occasions that he had effective command and control on the soldiers on the ground, including the military police, and all these brigades, and the other sub-units that we came into contact with in the Lasva area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, I'm going to move to another segment, and you can -- we'll finish with those photographs in a little bit -- and I'd like to talk to you just briefly about your experiences with the Vitezovi, and before we begin to that, I'd like to move to yet a new tape, Mr. Dubuisson, which I believe would be 436. Mr. President and Your Honours, this is a video clip that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the British Broadcasting Company, and if we can play it at this juncture? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go back on the screen? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He's the commander of one of the elite special forces units of the HVO in Vitez, Lasva area, called Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges how you met Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: First time I met him, I think was the evening of 11th, 12th of June. I didn't know his name then, but he was involved in the taking of several U.N. vehicles as hostages in the centre of Vitez on the night of the 11th, 12th, during which I was the liaison officer that organised the release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the night of the 11th and 12th of ...

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: June, I think it was, sir. Effectively, several vehicles on their way back from Zenica had been directed into the town centre of Vitez. Once there, mines had been placed around them and across the roads, and the local population came out in force to protest that, the ineffectiveness of UNPROFOR. During this particular time the BiH were shelling, decided to shell the centre of Vitez. I was sent by Colonel Alastair to try to negotiate for the release of the vehicles from the centre of Vitez area. During that time, it was late at night, 2.00 in the morning, a gentleman held a gun to my face and threatened to kill myself and my interpreter and refused to release the vehicles on the grounds that UNPROFOR was moving weapons and munitions on behalf of the Armija and that we're not supporting the HVO in the same manner. After a heated discussion, several tense minutes, I extracted from the area, after making sure everybody was safe in the vehicles, and went to the Hotel Vitez where members of the ECMM were being held in the basement. I spoke to Darko Gelic, asked him to get Colonel Blaskic out so we could discuss the matter, pointed out the fact that this was just serving to upset any UNPROFOR-HVO relations, and after a few hours and a period of time when the mortaring had subsided outside during which the hotel had been hit on one or two occasions, Darko Gelic came back to me with instructions that Colonel Blaskic had said that the vehicles were to be released. I went outside, supervised removal of the mines, and spoke to the local commander, a chap called Carlo Grabovac who was a battalion commander near the entrance to Vitez town centre who made sure that the population had dispersed and we were then allowed to escort the vehicles out of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you two photographs, one which is Exhibit 252 and this particular exhibit, which is the top one, which is part of the 433 series, if we can get both of those? Exhibit 252, can you take a look at that, Captain -- it's not coming up on the monitor for some reason. There we go. Do you recognise the individual facing --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's Carlo Grabovac. He's one of the battalion commanders of the Vitez brigade, i.e. he's subordinate to Mario Cerkez and he was one of the commanders he had to liaise closely with on the ground to be able to get the civilians dispersed who were in part responsible for holding the vehicles hostage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph that is in the series, 433, and what is that number? 11, and is Carlo Grabovac in that photograph as well?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He is indeed, sir, yes. He stood on my left or your right as you look at the photograph, and that's taken outside the cinema in Vitez, which was Mario Cerkez's, the brigade commander, headquarters which is about 100 metres away from the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this particular instance, you had Darko Kraljevic and his Vitezovi operating in conjunction with the Vitez brigade on the command of Cerkez and Carlo Grabovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Blaskic was the one that ordered the release of this convoy of U.N. vehicles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir. I was -- went straight to the top in terms of -- it was obvious that it was difficult to quell the situation at a local level, so I went straight to the head man, spoke to Darko, who then went to speak to Colonel Blaskic, and then after several discussions Darko eventually came back with permission that the vehicles should leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they obey?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Very soon afterwards, yeah, after I had supervised it, everybody doing what he had been instructed to doing by Darko Gelic, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they obeyed Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to this map briefly, which is the map marked 124 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps you're going to take a break here. This might be a time to take a break. We can start in about 20 or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing, and please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Now we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. If I can just move to the next exhibit, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 437.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, just briefly going through Exhibit 437, this is a depiction of the locations of the various events, about which you just discussed on the night of the 11th of June, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 1 is the area where the U.N. convoy was stopped by the HVO and the Vitezovi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the general location where you had a gun put in your face by Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2, does that indicate the place where mines were put across the road to prevent a BRITBAT Warrior from getting into Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, the road was cut off, mines were placed across, and there were civilians in area 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 3, you went and tried to get assistance of Carlo Grabovac who was headquartered in number 4; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The place where you got relief was from Blaskic in the Hotel Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this event took place before you had been formally introduced to Darko Kraljevic, I take it. Let me show you a document, Exhibit 422, if I may, Mr. Dubuisson? This is a document that is in both English and Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian. Now, this is a document that you saw while in theatre; is that right, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is one of several we saw produced by the Hotel Vitez, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And normally did you get such documents from Darko Gelic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I was the mail boy between Hotel Vitez and Colonel Alastair, and these things would then be disseminated accordingly to Kiseljak or wherever, depending on what the content was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 2, the distribution list on that document? Can you read that distribution list, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: All HVO brigades, all the independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd operational zone commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was Blaskic; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is Colonel Blaskic, sir, yes. Which included the MTD, which is -- I think it's the transport one. It could have been the artillery. The ones I'm familiar with are the last ones which are the 4th military police battalion which is Pasko Ljubesic and the guys based in the Hotel Vitez, the Vitezovi which is commanded by Darko Kraljevic, and TURTKO 2nd, which were another sort of elite offensive fighting force based around the Travnik, Novi Bila, Novi Travnik area, and lastly a chap called Djuti who was a local dodgy car salesman, criminal, entrepreneur, and also involved militarily in several things that went on, particularly around the Novi Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see how these individual units were used in the overall tactical structure of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We saw the same pattern throughout our tour in Bosnia, which was that the local brigades, either local militia, would maintain the military positions around the Lasva Valley, but when it came to any offensive action or any attacks by the BiH that required supplementary troops, then the 4th military police, or the Vitezovi, or the TURTKO, or the Jokeri, people like that would be put to use if there was any particular area, for example, if the BiH were making an advance or an attempted advance into the Lasva area, then one of those specialist units would be drafted in to substantiate and increase the strength of the local brigade and militia position in that particular area, and if there were any offensive activities, military operations taking place, those were not undertaken by the HVO brigades, the local militia in the area, but by those specialist units, the Vitezovi, the TURTKO, and the military police sub-units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider that the use of these independent units was intricately involved in the tactical strategy of the HVO in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely. They came under command of Colonel Blaskic and they were used in augmenting -- correction, wrong, in actually carrying out the HVO's military intention; establishing, strengthening, and regaining ground lost to the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take your point on ground lost to the BiH, and I direct your attention to the latter part of October of 1993. Omit October of 1993. Did you observe an instance when the Vitezovi came in for the goal of doing exactly what you did, take over ground lost to the BiH, and if so, tell the Judges what happened, what you observed, and what ultimately transpired?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was visiting one of the local battalion commanders in the area of Donji Vecerska, we sat drinking coffee, exchange the niceties of the day, I was there with my Muslim interpreter when a chap came in who was -- who became known to me as Darko Kraljevic, the leader of the Vitezovi. He took over the meeting. It was quite obvious to me that he was revered by the battalion commander who gave up his seat for Darko Kraljevic, and Kraljevic told me that he was here to take command of the HVO in this particular area, just to explain that the Sesilja (phoen) area had fallen to the BiH recently, and that Kraljevic was saying that he had been instructed to take charge of the situation and to regain the ground lost to the Armija in that particular brigade area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain, was this local commander in Donji Vecerska a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was indeed, sir. He was a battalion commander that came under the Vitez brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Kraljevic then came up headquarters in Donji Vecerska?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He did so. He took over the headquarters, and I had cause to meet him there on several occasions after that, and also to bump into him further south from that position, i.e., in the direction of the HVO positions that had been lost to the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these meetings that you had with Darko Kraljevic, on some occasion did you have a pistol contest with Darko Kraljevic that you won?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Darko is a very egocentric character, enjoys demonstrating his machismo and soldiering prowess. He challenged me to a pistol duel by way of me establishing myself with him as an equal, as it were, and I undertook the competition, won the competition, and he handed me over as a prize a .357 Smith & Wesson Magnum which contained dum-dum bullets that he claimed he had used during Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention back to Darko in October of 1993, and if I can move to these two exhibits, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 438 for the part of the exhibit which comes from Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going with 438 first. There is a particular building circled in that exhibit. Is that the building that you circled as the location of the Vitezovi when you were there in October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
